prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its glucose-dependent actions on insulin secretion and appetite, which enabled incretin-based therapy of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked B049 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The scientific case is that it is a complete discovery arc: the incretin effect in humans (Holst), the identification of the biologically active truncated GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov), and the proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor pharmacology (Drucker). That arc led to medicines whose benefit is now shown in large randomized outcome trials for cardiovascular and renal disease as well as glycaemia and weight. It is a clear physiological finding with a clear mechanism, independently confirmed for decades, and with exceptional and still growing impact. No other shortlisted ballot combines mechanism, translation and population-level evidence at this scale. I keep Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because the prize should recognize who established the physiology and the active peptide rather than who built the industrial product.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The three-person limit forces the exclusion of Knudsen, whose long-acting acylated analogues made the drugs practical, and of early contributors such as Habener who are not in the credited set. Mojsov's priority relative to others working on the active GLP-1 form is debated, and I rely on the supplied credit and general knowledge of the history rather than an audited record. If the committee judges that the prize should reward the drug and not the hormone, my configuration is weaker and Sandberg's variant becomes more defensible. There is also a fair worry that a candidate this prominent makes the call too easy, and that easy calls deserve more scrutiny, not less.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen so that the prize spans physiology through therapeutics, and treats Mojsov as an important early contributor who is hard to include.
responses.response: I accept that Knudsen's acylation strategy is what made once-daily and once-weekly dosing possible, and that without it the hormone biology would not have reached patients at this scale. But this prize has usually honoured the discovery that opened the field, and the active peptide that Mojsov identified is the entity every later drug is built on. Drug-development credit is real, yet it is the part of the story that rests on a large industrial team and is the most contestable on those grounds. I would keep Mojsov over Knudsen, while conceding that this is a judgment about the purpose of the prize, not a fact about who did more work.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics second and notes that credit is spread over six names, so that any trio such as Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck.
responses.response: I agree that the importance of optogenetics is not in question, but I disagree that it is ready to be settled as a three-person prize. The channelrhodopsin discovery and the first demonstration of neuronal control are separate achievements, and there is a genuine argument that Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck have claims comparable to those of the names in the proposed trios. A trio that pairs the molecular discovery with one neuronal-application name will be hard to defend, so I rank it below CAR-T, where the central pair of June and Sadelain is cleaner. I would support it only if the molecular discovery were credited as its own achievement.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B014 second with June and Sadelain as a cleaner two-person set, and ranks B022 (cGAS-STING) fourth while noting that therapeutic payoff is not yet realized.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person set for CAR-T and share the view that Rosenberg's work belongs to a distinct line, adoptive cell therapy. On cGAS-STING the mechanism is clean and the Chen and Barber contributions are sharply defined, so the lack of an approved therapy does not disqualify it in principle; many basic-science prizes had no drug at the time. But in a year when B049 and B014 are available it does not need to compete, and I would let more clinical evidence accumulate before putting it forward.

responses.point: Svenningsson also ranks B049 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and B014 second with June and Sadelain, and notes that Eshhar, who first described the chimeric receptor concept, is absent from the supplied credit.
responses.response: We are nearly aligned, and the Eshhar issue is the right one to press. If the committee cannot credit the originator of the chimeric receptor concept, the CAR-T citation has to be worded around the clinical and costimulatory advances, which makes it a narrower achievement than the title suggests. That is a reason to prefer a single-part B049 prize this year and to treat B014 as the strongest alternative rather than a co-equal second part, which would also force awkward exclusions within the three-name cap.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen is the better third name alongside Drucker and Holst, and whether the supplied credit adequately reflects the contributions of Habener and others.
Whether the committee wants a single prize for B049 or a two-part prize pairing it with CAR-T, given that the three-person cap would then split the names awkwardly.
How to handle the absence of Eshhar from the CAR-T credited names if B014 is raised in later rounds.
The attribution evidence I used comes from the supplied credit and general knowledge, not from independent verification of priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted ballots. I co-authored the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and have co-authors such as Castelo-Branco, Betsholtz, Ernfors, Frisen, Lundeberg and Kharchenko, plus eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, but none of these is a credited name or a topic on the shortlist. Shared Karolinska affiliation with colleagues is not treated as a conflict.
